items.stem: Now think of an interesting story about your patterns. Compare your patterns with the patterns drawn by your friends. Are the patterns same or different? Narrate your story to others and listen to their stories. Do you notice that everyone’s patterns, names and stories are different? Is it not fun?
items.answer: 1. I looked at the star map and joined some stars to make a pattern that looked like a fish.

items.stem: Once you identify the Big Dipper, try to locate the Pole Star. Look at the two stars present at the end of the Big Dipper’s cup and imagine a straight line passing through these towards the north. At about five times the distance between these two stars, the imaginary line will lead to another star which is not very bright. This star is the Pole Star. You may also locate the bright constellation Orion and the star Sirius in the night sky.
items.answer: 1. I went outside at around 9 p.m. and looked towards the northern sky.

items.stem: Once you identify Orion, it is easy to locate the very bright star Sirius which is located close to Orion. Imagine a straight line passing through the three middle stars of Orion and look along this line towards the east. This will lead to Sirius.
items.answer: 1. I looked for Orion in the sky after sunset in January, facing the southern sky.

items.stem: When you are viewing at dusk, look for it near the Western direction after sunset. While many of the objects in the sky can be seen with our naked eyes directly, we can see them brighter and larger using a pair of binoculars or an instrument called a telescope (Figure). A telescope also helps us view many dim objects not visible by our naked eyes directly. Figure : A telescope You may get an opportunity to view the sky through a telescope whenever a night sky watching event is organized in your region.
items.answer: (i) I tried to spot Venus early in the morning before sunrise and saw a bright star-like object in the eastern sky—that was Venus, also called the Morning Star. (ii) One evening after sunset, I looked in the western sky and found the same bright object again—it was Venus acting as the Evening Star. (iii) Later, I attended a night sky event with a telescope. It showed me craters on the Moon, Jupiter’s moons, and Saturn’s rings—which we can’t see with the naked eye. (iv) I learned that telescopes make distant and faint space objects easier to see and study. (v) These activities helped me understand how planets, stars, and other objects appear in the sky. It was an exciting experience!

items.stem: (i) Solve the following riddle. My first alphabet is in MAN but not in CAN My second alphabet is in ACE and also in FAN My third alphabet is in RAT and not in CAT My fourth alphabet is in SUN but not in FUN I am a planet that moves around the Sun. (ii) Make two similar riddles by yourself.
items.answer: (i) MARS (ii) STAR, MOON

items.stem: Which of the following is not a member of our Solar System? (i) Sirius (ii) Comets (iii) Asteroids (iv) Pluto
items.answer: (i) Sirius Sirius is a star located outside our Solar System, in the constellation Canis Major. Comets and asteroids are small bodies that revolve around the Sun and are part of the Solar System. Pluto was once a planet and is now considered a dwarf planet, but still belongs to our Solar System.

items.stem: Which of the following is not a planet of the Sun? (i) Jupiter (ii) Pluto (iii) Neptune (iv) Saturn
items.answer: (ii) Pluto Pluto was once considered the ninth planet but is now classified as a dwarf planet by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). So, it is not counted as a main planet of the Sun in the Solar System.

items.stem: Which is the brighter star, the Pole Star or Sirius?
items.answer: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky. Although the Pole Star (Polaris) is important for navigation, Sirius shines much more brightly and is clearly visible in the constellation Canis Major.

items.stem: An artist’s representation of the Solar System is given in Figure. Is the order of the planets correct? If not, write the correct order in the boxes in the figure.
items.answer: The order of the planets in the figure may not be correct. The correct order from the Sun is: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.This is the scientifically accepted order of the 8 planets in the Solar System based on their increasing distance from the Sun.

items.stem: A portion of night sky with stars is shown in Figure . Look carefully and identify the groups of stars that form the patterns the Big Dipper and the Little Dipper. Draw lines to connect the stars for these patterns and label them. Also, identify and label the Pole Star. You may refer to Figure for help.
items.answer: 8. A portion of the night sky is shown in Figure. Draw lines to connect the stars for Orion and label the star Sirius. You may refer to Figure .

items.stem: A portion of the night sky is shown in Figure. Draw lines to connect the stars for Orion and label the star Sirius. You may refer to Figure .
items.answer: 9. You can see stars fading away at dawn and appearing at dusk. During the day we do not see the stars. Explain why.

items.stem: You can see stars fading away at dawn and appearing at dusk. During the day we do not see the stars. Explain why.
items.answer: We do not see stars during the day because the light from the Sun is very bright. This bright sunlight scatters in the atmosphere and overpowers the dim light of the stars. Although stars are still present in the sky during the day, they become invisible due to the Sun’s brightness.

items.stem: During a clear night, try to observe the Big Dipper 3–4 times at an interval of 2 to 3 hours. Also try to locate the Pole Star each time. Does the Big Dipper appear to move? Draw a rough sketch to illustrate this, mentioning the time in each case.
items.answer: When observed several times during the night, the Big Dipper appears to change its position in the sky. This is because of the rotation of the Earth on its axis.

items.stem: Think about the night sky and write a poem or a story on it.
items.answer: In the sky so deep and wide, Shining stars in the night abide. Orion hunts with bow so bright, While Sirius guards with steady light. The Big Dipper swings in silent grace, Around the Pole Star’s glowing face. I watch the sky and dream away, Of galaxies where night holds sway.

items.stem: What is a constellation, as traditionally understood and commonly used?

options.label: A
options.text: A single, very bright star in the night sky

options.label: B
options.text: A region of the sky containing only planets

options.label: C
options.text: A group of stars that appear to form a recognizable pattern or shape

options.label: D
options.text: An instrument used for observing distant stars

items.answer: (C) A group of stars that appear to form a recognizable pattern or shape. Traditionally, constellations refer to apparent groupings of stars that form imaginary outlines or patterns, often representing animals, mythological figures, or objects, which help in navigating the night sky.

items.stem: What is the name of the brightest star in the night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major?

options.label: A
options.text: Betelgeuse (Ardra)

options.label: B
options.text: Polaris (Pole Star)

options.label: C
options.text: Sirius

options.label: D
options.text: Aldebaran (Rohini)

items.answer: (C) Sirius The Sirius, found in the constellation Canis Major (the Great Dog), as the brightest star visible in our night sky.

items.stem: Why was recognizing star patterns and constellations a useful skill in olden times, especially for sailors and travellers?

options.label: A
options.text: It helped them predict the weather accurately

options.label: B
options.text: It was primarily used for telling time during the day

options.label: C
options.text: It helped them in finding directions (navigation) at sea or on land

options.label: D
options.text: It was mainly for creating horoscopes and astrological charts

items.answer: (C) It helped them in finding directions (navigation) at sea or on land. Before modern technology like GPS or magnetic compasses, specific star patterns and constellations served as reliable guides for navigation, helping travellers determine directions like North.

items.stem: According to the International Astronomical Union (IAU), how many constellations officially divide the entire sky?

options.label: A
options.text: 44 constellations

options.label: B
options.text: 66 constellations

options.label: C
options.text: 88 constellations

options.label: D
options.text: 102 constellations

items.answer: (C) 88 constellations To standardize celestial mapping, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) officially defined 88 constellations, which together cover the entire celestial sphere, each occupying a specific region of the sky.

items.stem: Which constellation is often represented as a hunter, with three stars in the middle forming its belt?

options.label: A
options.text: Taurus (the Bull)

options.label: B
options.text: Canis Major (the Great Dog)

options.label: C
options.text: Orion (the Hunter)

options.label: D
options.text: Ursa Minor (the Little Dipper)

items.answer: (C) Orion (the Hunter) The constellation Orion is famously depicted as a hunter. A distinctive feature is a short line of three bright stars that represent the hunter’s belt.

items.stem: What causes light pollution in big cities, making it difficult to see many stars in the night sky?

options.label: A
options.text: Too much natural moonlight

options.label: B
options.text: Excessive artificial light at night time, along with smoke and dust

options.label: C
options.text: The reflection of starlight from tall buildings

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the number of dim stars

items.answer: (B) Excessive artificial light at night time, along with smoke and dust. Light pollution refers to the brightening of the night sky caused by artificial light sources (streetlights, buildings, etc.). This, combined with atmospheric smoke and dust, scatters light and reduces the visibility of fainter stars.

items.stem: If you want to locate the Pole Star (Polaris) using the Big Dipper, what is the general method described?

options.label: A
options.text: Follow a line through the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper’s handle

options.label: B
options.text: Imagine a straight line passing through the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper’s cup, extending it about five times their distance

options.label: C
options.text: Look for the brightest star directly in the middle of the Big Dipper

options.label: D
options.text: The Pole Star is the middle star in the handle of the Big Dipper

items.answer: (B) Imagine a straight line passing through the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper’s cup, extending it about five times their distance. The two stars forming the outer edge of the Big Dipper’s cup are often called pointer stars. Extending an imaginary line through them northwards leads to the Pole Star.

items.stem: What is a key difference between the Sun and other stars as they appear from Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: The Sun emits light, while other stars only reflect light

options.label: B
options.text: The Sun appears much bigger and brighter because it is the star closest to us

options.label: C
options.text: Other stars are always hotter than the Sun

options.label: D
options.text: The Sun is a planet, while other stars are gaseous bodies

items.answer: (B) The Sun appears much bigger and brighter because it is the star closest to us. The Sun is a star, just like the distant stars we see at night. Its apparent size and brightness are due to its relative proximity to Earth compared to other stars, which are vastly farther away.

items.stem: What is the Sun?

options.label: A
options.text: A very large planet reflecting light

options.label: B
options.text: A constellation of many small stars

options.label: C
options.text: A star, an extremely hot spherical ball of gases that produces its own light and heat

options.label: D
options.text: A large moon orbiting the Earth

items.answer: (C) A star, an extremely hot spherical ball of gases that produces its own light and heat. The Sun is classified as a star. It is a massive, luminous sphere of hot gases (primarily hydrogen and helium) that generates its own energy through nuclear fusion.

items.stem: Approximately how far is the Sun from the Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: 150 thousand km

options.label: B
options.text: 1.5 million km

options.label: C
options.text: 150 million km

options.label: D
options.text: 15 billion km

items.answer: (C) 150 million km The distance of the Sun from the Earth is about 150 million kilo metres. This distance is also defined as one astronomical unit (au).

items.stem: Why do other stars appear as mere points of light in the night sky, even though some are much bigger than our Sun?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they are much colder than our Sun

options.label: B
options.text: Because they are vastly farther away from Earth than our Sun

options.label: C
options.text: Because they do not produce their own light

options.label: D
options.text: Because Earth’s atmosphere blocks most of their light

items.answer: (B) Because they are vastly farther away from Earth than our Sun. The immense distances to other stars cause them to appear as tiny points of light, despite their potentially large actual sizes. Our Sun appears large because it is relatively very close.

items.stem: What is a planet?

options.label: A
options.text: A small, rocky object that orbits a planet

options.label: B
options.text: A collection of stars forming a recognizable pattern

options.label: C
options.text: A large, nearly spherical object that revolves around a star (like the Sun)

options.label: D
options.text: A celestial body that emits its own light

items.answer: (C) A large, nearly spherical object that revolves around a star (like the Sun). A planet is defined as a celestial body that orbits a star (in our case, the Sun), is massive enough for its own gravity to round it into a nearly spherical shape, and has cleared its orbital neighborhood (though this last part is a more modern IAU addition not fully detailed for this grade level).

items.stem: Which planet is known as the Red Planet because its soil is reddish in colour?

options.label: A
options.text: Venus

options.label: B
options.text: Mars

options.label: C
options.text: Jupiter

options.label: D
options.text: Earth

items.answer: (B) Mars Mars appears reddish due to the presence of iron oxide (rust) in its soil and rocks, earning it the nickname Red Planet.

items.stem: How do the inner four planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) generally differ from the outer four planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) in our Solar System?

options.label: A
options.text: Inner planets are larger and gaseous; outer planets are smaller and rocky

options.label: B
options.text: Inner planets are smaller and have solid, rocky surfaces; outer planets are much larger and mostly gaseous

options.label: C
options.text: Inner planets all have rings; outer planets do not

options.label: D
options.text: Inner planets are colder; outer planets are hotter

items.answer: (B) Inner planets are smaller and have solid, rocky surfaces; outer planets are much larger and mostly gaseous. The Solar System has a clear division: the inner planets are relatively small, dense, and terrestrial (rocky). The outer planets are gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) or ice giants (Uranus, Neptune), significantly larger and less dense.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the eight planets in our Solar System?

options.label: A
options.text: Mercury

options.label: B
options.text: Earth

options.label: C
options.text: Pluto

options.label: D
options.text: Neptune

items.answer: (C) Pluto Pluto was formerly classified as the ninth planet but was reclassified as a dwarf planet by the IAU in 2006. The eight official planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

items.stem: If you are observing the sky at dawn and see a very bright, star-like object near the Eastern horizon, which planet is it most likely to be?

options.label: A
options.text: Mars

options.label: B
options.text: Jupiter

options.label: C
options.text: Venus

options.label: D
options.text: Saturn

items.answer: (C) Venus Venus is often visible as a very bright object in the eastern sky before sunrise (as the Morning Star) or in the western sky after sunset (as the Evening Star) due to its orbit being closer to the Sun than Earth’s.

items.stem: How can one generally distinguish a planet from a star when observing the night sky with the naked eye?

options.label: A
options.text: Planets are always much dimmer than stars

options.label: B
options.text: Stars appear to twinkle a lot, while planets usually do not (or twinkle less)

options.label: C
options.text: Planets always appear larger than stars to the naked eye

options.label: D
options.text: Stars move rapidly across the sky, while planets remain stationary

items.answer: (B) Stars appear to twinkle a lot, while planets usually do not (or twinkle less). The twinkling effect of stars is due to Earth’s atmospheric turbulence distorting their point-like light. Planets, being closer, appear as tiny discs, and their light is less affected by this turbulence, so they tend to shine more steadily.

items.stem: What are natural satellites of planets commonly called?

options.label: A
options.text: Asteroids

options.label: B
options.text: Comets

options.label: C
options.text: Moons

options.label: D
options.text: Stars

items.answer: (C) Moons Celestial bodies that naturally orbit planets are called their natural satellites. The most common term for these natural satellites is moons. Earth has one Moon.

items.stem: Approximately how long does Earth’s Moon take to complete one revolution around the Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: About 24 hours

options.label: B
options.text: About 7 days

options.label: C
options.text: About 27 days

options.label: D
options.text: About 365 days

items.answer: (C) About 27 days The Moon completes one orbit around the Earth in approximately 27.3 days (its sidereal period).

items.stem: What are the circular bowl-like structures observed on the Moon’s surface called, and how were most of them formed?

options.label: A
options.text: Valleys, formed by water erosion

options.label: B
options.text: Mountains, formed by volcanic activity

options.label: C
options.text: Craters, formed by the impact of asteroids or rocks from space

options.label: D
options.text: Canals, believed to be man-made

items.answer: (C) Craters, formed by the impact of asteroids or rocks from space. The Moon’s surface is characterized by numerous craters. These are predominantly impact craters, formed when meteoroids, asteroids, or comets collided with the lunar surface.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Stars shine with their own light. Reason (R) : Stars are extremely hot, spherical balls of gases that produce a huge amount of energy.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Stars, including our Sun, generate their own light and heat through nuclear fusion processes occurring within their hot, dense cores. This energy production is what makes them luminous.

items.stem: Comets and asteroids

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

items.answer: (D) 1, 2, and 3 Our Solar System comprises the Sun (a star), the eight planets orbiting it, the moons (natural satellites) of these planets, as well as smaller bodies like asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets.

items.stem: An astronomer is using a telescope to view celestial objects. They are able to see faint objects that are not visible to the naked eye and observe details on planets more clearly. The primary function of the telescope in this context is:

options.label: A
options.text: To change the color of the celestial objects

options.label: B
options.text: To make distant objects appear brighter, larger, and more detailed

options.label: C
options.text: To measure the temperature of the stars

options.label: D
options.text: To listen to sounds from space

items.answer: (B) To make distant objects appear brighter, larger, and more detailed. Telescopes are optical instruments designed to collect more light than the human eye and magnify the image of distant objects, allowing for the observation of fainter objects and finer details.

items.stem: What is the name of India’s first mission to the Moon, launched in 2008?

options.label: A
options.text: Mangalyaan

options.label: B
options.text: Chandrayaan-1

options.label: C
options.text: Gaganyaan

options.label: D
options.text: Aditya-L1

items.answer: (B) Chandrayaan-1 India’s first mission to the Moon, Chandrayaan-1, was launched in 2008 to study the Moon.

items.stem: What are asteroids?

options.label: A
options.text: Large gaseous planets found in the outer Solar System

options.label: B
options.text: Small, rocky, and irregularly shaped objects that revolve around the Sun, many found between Mars and Jupiter

options.label: C
options.text: Objects with long tails made of dust, gases, rocks, and ice that orbit the Sun

options.label: D
options.text: Natural satellites that orbit planets like Earth and Mars

items.answer: (B) Small, rocky, and irregularly shaped objects that revolve around the Sun, many found between Mars and Jupiter. Asteroids are minor planets, primarily found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. They are smaller than planets, often irregularly shaped, and composed mainly of rock and metal.

items.stem: Why does a comet develop a tail as it approaches the Sun?

options.label: A
options.text: The Sun’s gravity pulls material off the comet

options.label: B
options.text: The frozen material (ice) in the comet starts evaporating due to the Sun’s heat, forming the tail

options.label: C
options.text: The comet starts spinning rapidly, flinging off dust and gas

options.label: D
options.text: The comet collides with smaller asteroids, creating a debris trail

items.answer: (B) The frozen material (ice) in the comet starts evaporating due to the Sun’s heat, forming the tail. Comets are icy bodies. As they near the Sun, solar radiation heats them, causing the ices to vaporize (sublimate) and release gas and dust. This material is then pushed away by solar wind and radiation pressure, forming the characteristic tail.

items.stem: Which famous comet appears approximately every 76 years?

options.label: A
options.text: Comet Hale-Bopp

options.label: B
options.text: Halley’s Comet

options.label: C
options.text: Comet ISON

options.label: D
options.text: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9

items.answer: (B) Halley’s Comet Halley’s Comet as a famous example, noting its periodic appearance roughly every 76 years.

items.stem: What is the Milky Way Galaxy?

options.label: A
options.text: The collection of all planets in our Solar System

options.label: B
options.text: A large cloud of gas and dust where new stars are formed

options.label: C
options.text: Our home galaxy, a vast system containing millions to billions of stars, including our Solar System

options.label: D
options.text: A particularly bright constellation visible throughout the year

items.answer: (C) Our home galaxy, a vast system containing millions to billions of stars, including our Solar System. The Milky Way Galaxy is the barred spiral galaxy that contains our Solar System. It appears as a faint band of light across the night sky and is composed of countless stars, gas, and dust.

items.stem: What is the primary difference between how planets and stars produce light (as seen from Earth)?

options.label: A
options.text: Planets produce their own light; stars reflect sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Stars produce their own light; planets primarily shine by reflecting sunlight

options.label: C
options.text: Both planets and stars produce their own light equally

options.label: D
options.text: Neither planets nor stars produce light; they reflect light from the Moon

items.answer: (B) Stars produce their own light; planets primarily shine by reflecting sunlight. Stars are self-luminous bodies that generate light through nuclear fusion. Planets do not produce their own significant light; they are visible because they reflect the light from their parent star (in our case, the Sun).

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a primary reason why the night sky in Nubra, Ladakh is very clearly visible?

options.label: A
options.text: Almost cloudless weather

options.label: B
options.text: Almost no air pollution

options.label: C
options.text: Almost no light pollution

options.label: D
options.text: The presence of many artificial lights for better viewing

items.answer: (D) The presence of many artificial lights for better viewing. The clear visibility of the night sky in Nubra is attributed to its clear weather, and lack of air and light pollution. Artificial lights would cause light pollution, hindering night sky observation.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Pole Star appears stationary in the North direction in the Northern Hemisphere. Reason (R) : The Pole Star is located very close to the Earth’s axis of rotation when extended into space.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The Pole Star (Polaris) appears nearly stationary because it lies almost directly above the Earth’s North Celestial Pole, the point around which the northern sky appears to rotate due to Earth’s rotation.

items.stem: To get the best view of a faint constellation, what kind of night and location should an observer choose?

options.label: A
options.text: A moonlit night in the middle of a brightly lit city

options.label: B
options.text: A cloudy night in a rural area

options.label: C
options.text: A clear, moonless night in an open area away from city lights

options.label: D
options.text: A clear night, but only during twilight hours

items.answer: (C) A clear, moonless night in an open area away from city lights. For optimal night sky viewing, especially for faint objects, conditions should minimize interference. This means a clear sky (no clouds), no bright moonlight, and a location with minimal light pollution (away from city lights).

items.stem: The Indian term nakshatra is used in astronomy to denote:

options.label: A
options.text: Only planets visible to the naked eye

options.label: B
options.text: Either a certain star or a group of stars (like Ardra or Krittika)

options.label: C
options.text: The path of the Sun across the sky

options.label: D
options.text: Only the phases of the Moon

items.answer: (B) Either a certain star or a group of stars (like Ardra or Krittika). The More to know! box explains that in Indian astronomy, nakshatra refers to specific stars or asterisms (small groups of stars), such as Ardra (Betelgeuse) and Krittika (Pleiades).

items.stem: Why is it important to wait for about half an hour for eyes to get adjusted to darkness before night sky watching?

options.label: A
options.text: To allow the stars to become brighter

options.label: B
options.text: To allow the pupils of the eyes to dilate, increasing sensitivity to faint light

options.label: C
options.text: To give time for clouds to clear away

options.label: D
options.text: To allow the telescope to cool down to the ambient temperature

items.answer: (B) To allow the pupils of the eyes to dilate, increasing sensitivity to faint light. When moving from a bright to a dark environment, the pupils of the eyes enlarge (dilate) to let in more light. This process, called dark adaptation, takes time and significantly improves the ability to see faint objects like stars.

items.stem: What is the movement of an object, like a planet, around another much larger object, like the Sun, called?

options.label: A
options.text: Rotation

options.label: B
options.text: Revolution

options.label: C
options.text: Constellation

options.label: D
options.text: Galaxy

items.answer: (B) Revolution Revolution refers to the orbital motion of one celestial body around another. For example, planets revolve around the Sun, and moons revolve around planets.

items.stem: Which of these is Earth’s natural satellite?

options.label: A
options.text: Mars

options.label: B
options.text: The Sun

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon

options.label: D
options.text: Sirius

items.answer: (C) The Moon The Moon is the only natural satellite that orbits the Earth. It is our closest celestial neighbor.

items.stem: What is a key difference between the surface of Earth and the surface of the Moon regarding atmosphere and life?

options.label: A
options.text: Earth has a thick atmosphere and abundant life; the Moon has hardly any atmosphere and no known life

options.label: B
options.text: Both have thick atmospheres, but only Earth has life

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon has a denser atmosphere than Earth, supporting simple life forms

options.label: D
options.text: Neither Earth nor the Moon has a significant atmosphere or life

items.answer: (A) Earth has a thick atmosphere and abundant life; the Moon has hardly any atmosphere and no known life. Earth possesses a substantial atmosphere and harbors a vast diversity of life. The Moon, in contrast, has a very tenuous exosphere (hardly any atmosphere) and no evidence of indigenous life.

items.stem: Which of these planets is NOT one of the inner four planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars)?

options.label: A
options.text: Venus

options.label: B
options.text: Earth

options.label: C
options.text: Jupiter

options.label: D
options.text: Mars

items.answer: (C) Jupiter The inner four planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. Jupiter is the first of the outer planets, a gas giant located beyond the asteroid belt.

items.stem: If astronomers discover a new celestial body orbiting a star other than our Sun, what would this newly discovered body be called?

options.label: A
options.text: A moon of our Solar System

options.label: B
options.text: An asteroid within our Solar System

options.label: C
options.text: An explanted

options.label: D
options.text: A new constellation

items.answer: (C) An explanted. Planets that orbit stars outside of our own Solar System are termed explants or extra solar planets. The search for explants is a major area of modern astronomical research.

items.stem: In which Indian region, known for its clear skies and low pollution, do Yangdol and Dorjay live?

options.label: A
options.text: The Sunder bans, West Bengal

options.label: B
options.text: The Rann of Kutch, Gujarat

options.label: C
options.text: Nubra, Ladakh

options.label: D
options.text: The Western Ghats, Kerala

items.answer: (C) Nubra, Ladakh The Yangdol and Dorjay as residents of a village in Nubra, Ladakh, a region praised for its majestic mountains and exceptionally clear night skies ideal for stargazing.

items.stem: Why do stars, which are massive celestial bodies, appear as tiny points of light from Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they are actually very small in size

options.label: B
options.text: Because Earth’s atmosphere filters out most of their light

options.label: C
options.text: Because they are extremely far away from Earth

options.label: D
options.text: Because they emit very little light compared to the Sun

items.answer: (C) Because they are extremely far away from Earth. The vast interstellar distances make even enormous stars appear as small points of light when viewed from Earth. Their apparent smallness is due to their immense distance, not their actual size.

items.stem: What is the term for the Earth’s movement around the Sun?

options.label: A
options.text: Rotation

options.label: B
options.text: Revolution

options.label: C
options.text: Constellation

options.label: D
options.text: Libration

items.answer: (B) Revolution Revolution refers to the orbital motion of one celestial body around another. The Earth revolves around the Sun, completing one orbit in approximately one year.

items.stem: Which planet is commonly called the Morning Star or Evening Star because it shines brightly at dawn or dusk?

options.label: A
options.text: Mars

options.label: B
options.text: Jupiter

options.label: C
options.text: Venus

options.label: D
options.text: Mercury

items.answer: (C) Venus Venus is often the brightest planet visible in the sky and can be seen shining brilliantly in the east before sunrise (Morning Star) or in the west after sunset (Evening Star).

items.stem: What is a significant visual difference between the inner four planets (e.g., Earth, Mars) and the outer four planets (e.g., Jupiter, Saturn) regarding their structure?

options.label: A
options.text: Inner planets are gaseous; outer planets are rocky

options.label: B
options.text: Inner planets have solid, rocky surfaces; outer planets are mostly gaseous and much larger

options.label: C
options.text: Inner planets all have prominent rings; outer planets do not

options.label: D
options.text: Inner planets are much farther from the Sun than outer planets

items.answer: (B) Inner planets have solid, rocky surfaces; outer planets are much larger and mostly gaseous. The inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are terrestrial, meaning they have solid, rocky surfaces. The outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are gas giants or ice giants, lacking solid surfaces and being considerably larger.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of asteroids as described?

options.label: A
options.text: They are small objects in the Solar System

options.label: B
options.text: They are rocky and irregular in shape

options.label: C
options.text: They all have long, visible tails made of gas and dust

options.label: D
options.text: Many revolve around the Sun in a belt between Mars and Jupiter

items.answer: (C) They all have long, visible tails made of gas and dust. Asteroids are primarily rocky and metallic bodies. Long tails of gas and dust are characteristic of comets when they approach the Sun, not asteroids.

items.stem: If you were trying to identify the constellation Orion in the night sky during winter in India, what distinctive feature would you look for first?

options.label: A
options.text: A very bright single star isolated from others

options.label: B
options.text: A group of seven stars forming a dipper shape

options.label: C
options.text: Three bright stars in a short, straight line (Orion’s belt)

options.label: D
options.text: A faint, hazy patch of light stretching across the sky

items.answer: (C) Three bright stars in a short, straight line (Orion’s belt). The easiest way to find Orion is to first identify the three bright stars in a row that form its belt, a very recognizable asterism within the constellation.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : The Sun appears much larger and brighter than other stars. Reason (R) : The Sun is the largest and hottest star in the entire universe.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (C) A is true, but R is false. The Sun does appear much larger and brighter to us than other stars. However, this is because it is the closest star to Earth. There are many other stars in the universe that are much larger and hotter than our Sun.

items.stem: It revolves around the Earth.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

items.answer: (A) 1 and 2 only The Sun is indeed a star and is composed of extremely hot gases. However, the Earth revolves around the Sun, not the other way around.

items.stem: Yangdol and Dorjay are observing the night sky. They notice a celestial object with a long, glowing tail that slowly moves across the sky over several nights. This object is most likely a:

options.label: A
options.text: Planet like Venus

options.label: B
options.text: Constellation like Orion

options.label: C
options.text: Comet

options.label: D
options.text: Natural satellite like the Moon

items.answer: (C) Comet Comets are celestial bodies made of ice, dust, and rock that develop a visible tail of gas and dust when they approach the Sun. Their appearance in the sky is often temporary as they follow their orbits.

items.stem: What is the approximate distance of the Moon from the Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: 150 million km

options.label: C
options.text: 1.5 million km

items.answer: (B) 3,84,000 km The Moon is about 3,84,000 kilometres away from the Earth, making it our closest natural celestial neighbour.

items.stem: Why does the Pole Star (Dhruva tara) appear stationary in the sky from the Northern Hemisphere?

options.label: A
options.text: Because it is the brightest star and does not move

options.label: B
options.text: Because it is located very close to the Earth’s axis of rotation extended into the northern sky

options.label: C
options.text: Because it is much closer to Earth than any other star

options.label: D
options.text: Because it is part of a constellation that does not appear to move

items.answer: (B) Because it is located very close to the Earth’s axis of rotation extended into the northern sky. The Pole Star’s apparent fixed position is due to its alignment almost directly above the Earth’s North Celestial Pole. As the Earth rotates, this star appears to remain stationary while other stars seem to circle around it.

items.stem: What is the term used in Indian astronomy for either a certain star or a group of stars, such as Ardra or Krittika?

options.label: A
options.text: Rashi

options.label: B
options.text: Graha

options.label: C
options.text: Nakshatra

options.label: D
options.text: Dhumaketu

items.answer: (C) Nakshatra Nakshatra is an Indian astronomical term referring to specific stars or asterisms (star groups), like Ardra (Betelgeuse) or Krittika (Pleiades).

items.stem: The successful soft-landing of Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander on the Moon occurred on which date, now celebrated as National Space Day in India?

options.label: B
options.text: August 23, 2023

options.label: C
options.text: October 22, 2008

options.label: D
options.text: September 7, 2019

items.answer: (B) August 23, 2023 The Vikram lander of the Chandrayaan-3 mission successfully soft-landed on the Moon on August 23, 2023, and this date has been declared National Space Day in India.

items.stem: How does the Earth (Blue Planet) primarily get its blue appearance when viewed from space?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to its blue-colored rocks and soil

options.label: B
options.text: Due to a large portion of its surface being covered with water

options.label: C
options.text: Due to the reflection of blue light from its atmosphere

options.label: D
options.text: Due to the presence of blue vegetation

items.answer: (B) Due to a large portion of its surface being covered with water. The Earth is often called the Blue Planet because oceans and other water bodies cover a significant majority of its surface, giving it a predominantly blue appearance from space.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a condition mentioned as ideal for night sky watching?

options.label: A
options.text: A clear, cloudless night

options.label: B
options.text: A location in a brightly lit city center

options.label: C
options.text: An open area away from tall buildings and trees

options.label: D
options.text: A moonless night, especially for faint objects

items.answer: (B) A location in a brightly lit city center. Bright city lights cause light pollution, which obscures the view of fainter celestial objects. Ideal night sky watching requires dark locations away from such artificial lighting.

items.stem: A student is using a sky mapping app on their phone to identify constellations. The app shows a pattern of stars resembling a large ladle or plough in the northern sky. This is most likely the constellation commonly known as:

options.label: A
options.text: Orion

options.label: B
options.text: Canis Major

options.label: C
options.text: The Big Dipper (part of Ursa Major)

options.label: D
options.text: Taurus

items.answer: (C) The Big Dipper (part of Ursa Major) The Big Dipper is a well-known asterism (star pattern) within the constellation Ursa Major, easily recognizable by its shape resembling a ladle or plough, and it is prominent in the northern sky.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Planets shine by reflecting sunlight. Reason (R) : Planets, like stars, generate their own light through nuclear fusion.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (C) A is true, but R is false. Planets are visible because they reflect light from the Sun (or their host star). They do not generate their own light through nuclear fusion; that process is characteristic of stars.

items.stem: Its surface has craters formed by impacts.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 and 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

items.answer: (C) 1 and 3 only The Moon is Earth’s sole natural satellite and its surface is heavily catered due to impacts. It has hardly any atmosphere, unlike Earth’s thick atmosphere.

items.stem: An ancient caravan leader, traveling through the Nubra region at night without a compass, needs to determine the north direction. Which celestial object or pattern would be most reliable for finding the North direction?

options.label: A
options.text: The brightest star visible, Sirius

options.label: B
options.text: The constellation Orion

options.label: C
options.text: The Pole Star (Polaris/Dhruva tara)

options.label: D
options.text: The planet Venus when visible as the Morning Star

items.answer: (C) The Pole Star (Polaris/Dhruva tara). The Pole Star is renowned for its fixed position in the northern sky (in the Northern Hemisphere), making it an excellent and reliable indicator of the North direction for navigation.

items.stem: What did ancient caravans passing through Nubra use to find direction?
items.answer: They used particular stars in the clear skies.

items.stem: Do stars shine with their own light or reflected light?
items.answer: Stars shine with their own light.

items.stem: What are groups of stars that appear to form patterns called?
items.answer: These patterns are called constellations.

items.stem: How many constellations were officially listed by the International Astronomical Union (IAU)?
items.answer: 88 constellations were officially listed.

items.stem: Which star is the brightest in the night sky and is part of the Canis Major constellation?
items.answer: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.

items.stem: What is the Indian name for the Big Dipper constellation?
items.answer: The Big Dipper is known as Saptarishi in India.

items.stem: Which star appears stationary in the North direction in the Northern hemisphere?
items.answer: The Pole Star (Polaris or Dhruva tara).

items.stem: What is the presence of excessive artificial light at night time referred to as?
items.answer: It is referred to as light pollution.

items.stem: Is the Pole Star visible from the southern hemisphere of Earth?
items.answer: No, the Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere.

items.stem: What is the Sun primarily composed of?
items.answer: The Sun is an extremely hot spherical ball of gases.

items.stem: What is the approximate distance between the Sun and the Earth called?
items.answer: It is called an astronomical unit (au).

items.stem: What is the movement of an object around the Sun called?
items.answer: The movement of an object around the Sun is called revolution.

items.stem: Name the planet closest to the Sun.
items.answer: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.

items.stem: Which planet is commonly called the Red Planet?
items.answer: Mars is commonly called the Red Planet.

items.stem: What are the large, flat ring-like structures around planets like Saturn made of?
items.answer: They are made of dust particles and rocky material.

items.stem: What are natural satellites of planets commonly called?
items.answer: Natural satellites of planets are commonly called moons.

items.stem: How many moons does Earth have?
items.answer: Earth has one Moon.

items.stem: What are the bowl-like structures on the Moon’s surface called?
items.answer: These structures are called craters.

items.stem: What is the name of India’s home galaxy?
items.answer: India’s home galaxy is called the Milky Way Galaxy (or Akasha Ganga).

items.stem: What are planets discovered revolving around other stars in our galaxy called?
items.answer: They are called exoplanets.

items.stem: How did recognizing star patterns help people in olden times before modern technology?
items.answer: Recognizing star patterns helped people, particularly sailors and travellers, in finding directions at sea or on land for navigation.

items.stem: What is a constellation according to current definitions by the International Astronomical Union (IAU)?
items.answer: Currently, constellations are defined as regions of the sky, which include groups of stars that often form prominent patterns.

items.stem: Name the constellation often represented as a hunter and mention the feature representing his belt.
items.answer: The constellation Orion is often represented as a hunter. Three bright stars in a short straight line in the middle represent the hunter’s belt.

items.stem: What is the significance of the Pole Star for navigation in the Northern Hemisphere?
items.answer: The Pole Star appears stationary in the North direction, which consistently helps in locating the North direction, aiding navigation.

items.stem: Why might fewer stars be visible in a big city compared to a village on a clear night?
items.answer: Fewer stars are visible in big cities due to light pollution, smoke, and dust, which obscure the night sky.

items.stem: What is the Sun, and why does it glow so brightly?
items.answer: The Sun is a star, an extremely hot spherical ball of gases. It glows brightly because it gives out a huge amount of energy.

items.stem: Why does the Sun appear much bigger and brighter to us than other stars?
items.answer: The Sun appears much bigger and brighter because it is the star closest to us. Other stars are much farther away.

items.stem: What is a planet? Name the four inner planets of our Solar System.
items.answer: A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. The four inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

items.stem: Why is Venus often called the Morning Star or Evening Star?
items.answer: Venus is called the Morning Star or Evening Star because it usually shines brightly at dawn (morning) or dusk (evening).

items.stem: Why is Earth referred to as the Blue Planet?
items.answer: Earth is called the Blue Planet because a large portion of its surface is covered with water, making it appear blue from space.

items.stem: What are the general characteristics of the four outermost planets of our Solar System?
items.answer: The four outermost planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are much larger than Earth, are mostly made of gases, and have rings around them.

items.stem: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
items.answer: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its dense atmosphere traps a significant amount of heat, leading to a strong greenhouse effect.

items.stem: What is a natural satellite? Give an example from our Solar System.
items.answer: A natural satellite is an object that moves around a planet. Earth’s Moon is an example of a natural satellite.

items.stem: Briefly describe the surface of the Moon and what causes its cratered appearance.
items.answer: The Moon’s surface is rocky and shows circular bowl-like structures called craters. Most craters formed due to the impact of asteroids or rocks from space.

items.stem: What is an asteroid belt, and where is it located in our Solar System?
items.answer: An asteroid belt is a region where many small, rocky, and irregular-shaped objects called asteroids revolve around the Sun. It is located mainly between Mars and Jupiter.

items.stem: What are comets made of, and what causes them to develop a tail?
items.answer: Comets are made of dust, gases, rocks, and ice. As a comet approaches the Sun, its frozen material starts evaporating, forming the tail.

items.stem: What objects make up our Solar System?
items.answer: Our Solar System consists of the Sun, eight planets, their moons, and many smaller objects including asteroids and comets.

items.stem: What is the Milky Way Galaxy? What is our Solar System’s relation to it?
items.answer: The Milky Way Galaxy (Akasha Ganga) is a vast collection of millions to billions of stars. Our Solar System is a part of this galaxy.

items.stem: Why is it generally difficult to see other stars during the daytime?
items.answer: During the daytime, the extreme brightness of the Sun, which is much closer to us, overwhelms the faint light from distant stars, making them invisible.

items.stem: What was the significance of India’s Chandrayaan-3 mission?
items.answer: Chandrayaan-3’s Vikram lander successfully soft- landed near the Moon’s south pole, making India the first country to achieve this feat.

items.stem: Explain how constellations were useful to ancient civilizations and how they are defined today. Give an example of a constellation and a prominent star within or near it.
items.answer: Ancient civilizations used recognizable star patterns (constellations) for navigation, helping sailors and travellers find directions. Today, the IAU defines 88 constellations as specific regions of the sky, which include these traditional patterns. For example, the constellation Canis Major contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.

items.stem: What is light pollution? How does it affect our ability to observe the night sky, and what measures are being taken to preserve dark skies?
items.answer: Light pollution is the presence of excessive artificial light at night. It brightens the night sky, reducing the visibility of fainter stars and celestial objects. To preserve dark skies for enjoyment and research, some dark sky reserves and parks have been established where light pollution is controlled.

items.stem: Describe the Sun’s characteristics and its importance to Earth. Why does it appear different from other stars?
items.answer: The Sun is our closest star, a massive, extremely hot sphere of gases producing immense heat and light. It’s crucial for Earth as the main energy source, supporting life, driving climate, seasons, and the water cycle. It appears larger and brighter than other stars simply because it is much closer to us.

items.stem: List the eight planets of our Solar System in order from the Sun. Briefly differentiate between the inner and outer planets in terms of their general composition and size.
items.answer: Planets in order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The inner four (Mercury to Mars) are smaller, rocky, and have solid surfaces. The outer four (Jupiter to Neptune) are much larger gas giants, primarily composed of gases and liquids, and often have rings.

items.stem: What are moons (natural satellites)? Describe key features of Earth’s Moon, including its distance, revolution period, and surface characteristics.
items.answer: Moons are natural satellites that revolve around planets. Earth’s Moon is about 384,000 km away and takes roughly 27 days to orbit Earth. Its surface is rocky, lacks a significant atmosphere, and is heavily cratered due to impacts from space objects over billions of years.

items.stem: What are asteroids and comets? Describe their composition and typical locations or movements within the Solar System.
items.answer: Asteroids are small, rocky, irregularly shaped objects, many of which orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are composed of dust, gases, rocks, and ice. They typically originate from the outer Solar System and develop long tails as they approach the Sun due to evaporating materials.

items.stem: Explain how to locate the Pole Star using the Big Dipper constellation. Why is the Pole Star significant for navigation?
items.answer: To find the Pole Star using the Big Dipper, locate the two stars at the end of the Big Dipper’s cup. Imagine a straight line extending upwards from these two stars. The Pole Star is found along this line, at about five times the distance between these two pointer stars. It’s significant because it’s almost directly above Earth’s North Pole and appears stationary, providing a reliable indicator of North.

items.stem: What is a galaxy? Describe our home galaxy, the Milky Way, and its appearance in a dark night sky.
items.answer: A galaxy is a vast system containing millions to billions of stars, along with gas, dust, and dark matter, all held together by gravity. Our home galaxy is the Milky Way (Akasha Ganga). From a dark location, it appears as an extended, faint, glowing band of light stretching across the sky.

items.stem: What are some challenges and preparations involved in night sky watching? Mention at least three preparations for a good viewing experience.
items.answer: Challenges include light pollution, weather (clouds), and obstructions like buildings. Preparations: 1. Choose a dark, open location away from city lights. 2. Pick a clear, moonless night for better visibility of fainter objects. 3. Allow your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness to see more stars.

items.stem: Briefly discuss India’s Chandrayaan missions. What was a major achievement of Chandrayaan-3, and what is the aim of Chandrayaan-4?
items.answer: India has launched missions to study the Moon: Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Chandrayaan-2 (2019), and Chandrayaan-3 (2023). Chandrayaan-3 achieved a historic soft landing near the Moon’s little-explored south pole. The upcoming Chandrayaan-4 mission aims to bring back soil and rock samples from the Moon for further study.

items.stem: Yangdol and Dorjay are observing the night sky from their village in Ladakh. Yangdol points to a group of seven bright stars forming a ladle shape and calls it Saptarishi. Dorjay then uses two stars in this group to find a fainter star that seems to stay in the same place. (i) What is the common English name for the Saptarishi constellation (or asterism)? (ii) Which star is Dorjay trying to locate using the pointer stars of the Saptarishi? (iii) Why is this star important for someone trying to find their way at night in the Northern Hemisphere?
items.answer: (i) The common English name for Saptarishi is the Big Dipper. (ii) Dorjay is trying to locate the Pole Star (Polaris or Dhruva tara). (iii) This star is important because it appears almost stationary in the sky and is located very close to the North Celestial Pole, thus reliably indicating the North direction.

items.stem: A student is looking at the sky just after sunset and sees a very bright, star-like object in the west that does not twinkle much. Her sky map app identifies it as Venus. (i) Why might Venus be referred to as the Evening Star in this situation? (ii) What is a key difference in appearance that helps distinguish planets like Venus from stars? (iii) Is Venus producing its own light like a star? Explain.
items.answer: (i) Venus is referred to as the Evening Star because it is visible and shining brightly in the western sky shortly after sunset. (ii) Stars tend to twinkle noticeably, while planets like Venus usually shine with a steadier light. (iii) No, Venus does not produce its own light. It shines because it reflects sunlight from its surface, much like Earth’s Moon.

items.stem: Astronomers are studying a newly discovered celestial object that orbits the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. It is rocky, irregular in shape, and much smaller than a planet. (i) What type of celestial object is this likely to be? (ii) What is the name of the region where many such objects are found? (iii) If this object were primarily made of ice and dust and developed a long tail when it got closer to the Sun, what would it be called?
items.answer: (i) This object is likely to be an asteroid. (ii) The region where many such objects are found is called the asteroid belt. (iii) If it were made of ice and dust and developed a tail near the Sun, it would be called a comet.

items.stem: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully landed its Chandrayaan-3 mission near the Moon’s south pole. The Pragyan rover explored the surface, sending back data. (i) What is the Moon in relation to the Earth? (ii) Why is landing near the Moon’s south pole considered a significant achievement? (iii) Does the Moon have an atmosphere similar to Earth’s that could have affected the landing?
items.answer: (i) The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. (ii) The Moon’s south pole is a little-explored region, believed to contain water ice in permanently shadowed craters, making it scientifically valuable. (iii) No, the Moon has hardly any atmosphere, which means there is no air resistance to slow down a lander; different landing techniques are required.

items.stem: A group of students visits the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve in Ladakh. They are amazed by the clear view of a faint, milky band of light stretching across the entire sky. Their guide tells them it’s their home galaxy. (i) What is the name of this band of light, which is our home galaxy? (ii) What are galaxies primarily composed of? (iii) Why is a Dark Sky Reserve like Hanle particularly good for observing such celestial features?
items.answer: (i) This band of light is the Milky Way Galaxy (or Akasha Ganga). (ii) Galaxies are primarily composed of millions to billions of stars, along with gas, dust, and dark matter. (iii) A Dark Sky Reserve has minimal light pollution, meaning the sky is very dark, allowing faint celestial objects like the Milky Way to be seen clearly without interference from artificial lights.
